messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: pointers and casts in command.hpp
parts:
Now I'm looking at the code for command.hpp in the
current develop branch and see this:

template<class Sampler>
bool init_adapt(stan::mcmc::base_mcmc* sampler, categorical_argument* adapt) {

... snip ...

Sampler* s = dynamic_cast<Sampler*>(sampler);


Why wasn't this written to use argument inference as:

template <class Sampler>
bool
init_adpat(Sampler& sampler, ...

and then you don't need the dynamic cast. Or any cast.
And could it be declared const?


Same function, but now in the ...snip... part there's this:

double delta = dynamic_cast<real_argument*>(adapt->arg("delta"))->value();

Why is there a cast here? The problem with doing this this way
is that there's no compile-time guarantee of types.

Would there be a way to overload the arg method in adapt, and do something
like this:

init_adpat(Sampler& sampler, const categorical_argument& adapt) {
...
double delta = adapt.get_double("delta");

This eliminates the cast and all that cut-and-paste of arrows and
asterisks and parens (this pattern shows up all over the command.hpp
file).

Although this guarantees all the types, presumably the get_double()
method would have to throw an exception if it represented a value
that's not a double value.

Overall, it's very dangerous to be calling these arguments by
a string-based name any way you slice it. Even better would
be something like:

double delta = adapt.get_delta();

that's guaranteed to be well-defined and return the right type
of value. That then requires you to push more of the logic back
into the argument class.

- Bob

messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] pointers and casts in command.hpp
parts:
> Now I'm looking at the code for command.hpp in the
> current develop branch and see this:
>
> template<class Sampler>
> bool init_adapt(stan::mcmc::base_mcmc* sampler, categorical_argument* adapt) {
>
> ... snip ...
>
> Sampler* s = dynamic_cast<Sampler*>(sampler);
>
>
> Why wasn't this written to use argument inference as:
>
> template <class Sampler>
> bool
> init_adpat(Sampler& sampler, ...
>
> and then you don't need the dynamic cast. Or any cast.
> And could it be declared const?

The only issue is that you have to template everything -- which would necessitate
touching not just command.hpp but also the mcmc_writer at the very least.

Your mutating the sampler directly -- won't that explicitly prevent the use of const?

> Same function, but now in the ...snip... part there's this:
>
> double delta = dynamic_cast<real_argument*>(adapt->arg("delta"))->value();
>
> Why is there a cast here? The problem with doing this this way
> is that there's no compile-time guarantee of types.

You have to cast because the arg tree is navigated based on the base,
virtual class definition (I don't see a way to do this that would still
allow the recursive navigation). If you want to use an arg's derived behavior
after navigating then you have to cast back to the explicit class.

I don't disagree that there's no compile-time guarantee, but this code
is also not dynamic so there's no run-time case we haven't already
checked in the arg unit-tests.

>
> Would there be a way to overload the arg method in adapt, and do something
> like this:
>
> init_adpat(Sampler& sampler, const categorical_argument& adapt) {
> ...
> double delta = adapt.get_double("delta");
>
> This eliminates the cast and all that cut-and-paste of arrows and
> asterisks and parens (this pattern shows up all over the command.hpp
> file).
>
> Although this guarantees all the types, presumably the get_double()
> method would have to throw an exception if it represented a value
> that's not a double value.
>
> Overall, it's very dangerous to be calling these arguments by
> a string-based name any way you slice it. Even better would
> be something like:
>
> double delta = adapt.get_delta();
>
> that's guaranteed to be well-defined and return the right type
> of value. That then requires you to push more of the logic back
> into the argument class.

It's not just rearranging the logic -- it's completely changing the hierarchical
structure. Adapt is essentially a container class, and has no concept
of what it contains outside of a bunch of derived arg classes. In order
to write methods as you described above you would either have to
(a) hard code everything which would be a nightmare given the
combinatorics or (b) write get_double, get_string, etc for every container
class and then throw exceptions everywhere. In either case you're
undercutting the utility of the polymorphism.

Again, in practice this isn't an issue because the arg unit-tests run
every argument configuration so that we know there are no run-time
conflicts.

messages.author: a5e83218c834e013
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] pointers and casts in command.hpp
parts:
> I haven't even gone so far as to see what the return type
> of ->arg() is to understand why it needs to be cast to
> real_argument*.

Everything returns a pointer to the base argument class, which allows
for the tree to be traversed agnostic to the exact argument types (the
interface requires all the navigation methods be implemented). To
use any value-based info you have to cast up to the derived class.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-dev] pointers and casts in command.hpp

Given that everything's resolved statically, it seems
not impossible we could resolve the types statically.
Maybe with something like the CRTP.

Not a super high priority, of course.

And I wouldn't want a type monstrosity that's even
harder to follow just to satisfy my desire not to
use pointers (other than implicitly through refs)
or casts.

- Bob
